background.definition: Tropical sprue is condition marked by diarrhea, malabsorption, and multiple nutritional deficiencies. It is a diagnosis of exclusion.

list.listitem: The prevalence varies widely by location and by changes in diagnostic criteria over time.
Older studies indicate a 6% annual incidence in Puerto Rico.
Tropical sprue is endemic to tropical and subtropical regions, including the Caribbean, South America, Africa, South Asia, and East Asia.
Patient may have HLA type AW-19 series or HLA-B8.
No specific organism has been identified, but aerobic and anaerobic bacteria have been implicated, including Enterobacteriaceae species.
Risk factors include living or traveling to tropical or subtropical regions.
Small bowel bacterial overgrowth leads to villous atrophy and malabsorption of nutrients.
Screening asymptomatic patients is not recommended. C
There are no known preventive measures. C
Tropical sprue is a clinical diagnosis of diarrhea, malabsorption, and nutritional deficiency. There may be small bowel mucosal atrophy. It is a diagnosis of exclusion. C
D-xylose malabsorption is found 99% of patients, steatorrhea in 90%, and vitamin B12 malabsorption in 60%-90%. C

list.listitem: Typical symptoms inof tropical sprue clude chronic diarrhea and steatorrhea. The patient may present with abdominal pain, bloating or cramping, weight loss, and edema. Signs and symptoms of nutritional deficiencies may be present (especially folate, vitamin B12, and protein deficiencies).
In 40 expatriates living in the United States, the most common symptoms were anorexia (95%), diarrhea (88%), weight loss (88%), and weakness (88%).
In 31 patients in Africa, the most common signs were anemia (91%), moderate to severe weight loss (23%-55%), edema (26%), and pellagra skin changes (16%).
Fever is present in 25% of patients.
Order standard stool studies (ova and parasites, gram stain, and stool culture) to rule out other causes of acute diarrhea.
Order CBC; megaloblastic anemia is very common.
D-xylose malabsorption is found 99% of patients, steatorrhea in 90%, and vitamin B12 malabsorption in 60%-90%.
Although not necessary for the diagnosis, esophagogastroduodenoscopy and small bowel biopsies usually reveal moderate to severe villous atrophy (77%).
Suspect tropical sprue in a patient with a relevant travel or residential history and diarrhea, malabsorption, and nutritional deficiency.
Order stool studies and CBC to rule out other common causes.
Order vitamin B12 level, d-xylose absorption, and quantitative stool fat tests to determine if nutritional deficiencies are occurring.
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy is not necessary for diagnosis, but may help rule out other common causes.
Antibiotics, folic acid, and vitamin B12 are the mainstays of treatment. B
The durecommended ration of treatment for antibiotic and folic acid is 6 months. C
Prescribe tetracycline 250 mg 4 times daily or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus folic acid 5 mg daily for 6 months. Give vitamin B12 (0.1 mg daily) intramuscularly for 1 week.

Adequate folic acid absorption is needed for the treatment of megaloblastic anemia associated with tropical sprue; the use of antibiotics may affect small intestine absorptive capacity and increase absorption of folic acid.

Six months of poorly absorbed sulfonamides (Sulfasuxidine or sulfaguanidine) produced a clinical, gastroenterologic, and hematologic remission in 8 patients from Puerto Rico, similar to treatment with oxytetracycline. This may be an option for patients allergic to tetracyclines.
Not all patients will respond to antibiotics and folate therapy as seen in an Indian epidemic of tropical sprue, distinguishing it from its Caribbean counterpart.
Most patients treated for tropical sprue will recover. B
Patients with acute tropical sprue tend to have better outcomes than those with chronic symptoms after treatment. B
Patients with preexisting deficiencies of folate, vitamin B12, and/or protein may be at greater risk for the development of sprue, possibly by rendering the mucosa more susceptible to injury.
Children seem to be at a decreased risk for developing tropical sprue.
Tropical sprue in children is similar to that in adults and responds well to treatment.
